metadata.title: The Number I Was Proudest Of
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.source: inbox/term2-week04/term2-week4-video-content.md (Week 4); narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27)
metadata.note: Project update. Thesis: self-review catches local problems; outside review catches systemic ones — the headline 94.2% agreement is a routing statistic, so the paper now leads with 5.8% human adjudication. Credit: the critique came from the professor; CRITIQ helped make the fixes, it didn't find them; Janvi made the revisions. Only Professor Brown may be named; the critic is 'my professor'. WORDING LAW: 'verified' appears only as the word being removed.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure + critique credited to the professor.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about the hardest change to our paper: demoting the number I was proudest of. This narration is an AI-generated voice; the work is mine, and the critique that drove it came from my professor.

props.command: My professor sent a ten-item critique of our paper. How do I work through it?
props.segment: The Number I Was Proudest Of.
output: Sort the items by what each one needs

beats.role_note: Checklist of required sections ticking; new 'Gene Ontology' section card with four chips: the API · the category gate · the silent fallback · why GO over other ontologies.
beats.narration_text: First, I finished the journal's required sections, and wrote a new Gene Ontology section the paper had been missing: the API, the category gate, the silent fallback, and why Gene Ontology over other ontologies.
beats.visual_intent: Checklist of required sections ticking; new 'Gene Ontology' section card with four chips: the API · the category gate · the silent fallback · why GO over other ontologies.

beats.role_note: Critique card '10 items' → three bins: fixable with existing data · needs new experiments · needs professor input; first bin ticked 'this week · edits with CRITIQ'.
beats.narration_text: Then my professor sent a ten-item critique. I sorted it into three groups: fixable with data we had, needing new experiments, and needing a professor's input. I fixed the first group this week, using CRITIQ to make the edits.
beats.visual_intent: Critique card '10 items' → three bins: fixable with existing data · needs new experiments · needs professor input; first bin ticked 'this week · edits with CRITIQ'.

show.event: first group fixed this week, with CRITIQ

beats.role_note: Three swaps, old struck → new highlighted: verified → curated; a large language model → GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI); independently verified → internal quality control by two co-authors with domain expertise.
beats.narration_text: Some were wording. Verified became curated across the whole paper. A large language model became G P T four o mini, by name. And independently verified became internal quality control by two co-authors with domain expertise.
beats.visual_intent: Three swaps, old struck → new highlighted: verified → curated; a large language model → GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI); independently verified → internal quality control by two co-authors with domain expertise.

beats.role_note: Paper sections as strips: one sentence highlighted ('week one: one sentence'), then highlights spread across every section; caption 'self-review: local · outside review: systemic'.
beats.narration_text: In week one I'd fixed one oversold sentence. But verified was everywhere. It was the paper's whole claim. My professor saw the pattern I missed from inside. Self-review catches local problems; outside review catches systemic ones.
beats.visual_intent: Paper sections as strips: one sentence highlighted ('week one: one sentence'), then highlights spread across every section; caption 'self-review: local · outside review: systemic'.

beats.role_note: Headline '94.2% agreement' shrinks to a side label 'routing statistic'; new lead '5.8% of items required human adjudication'.
beats.narration_text: The hardest change was the headline. The paper was built around 94.2 percent agreement. My professor called it a routing statistic, not a quality metric. Now the paper leads with this: 5.8 percent of items required human adjudication.
beats.visual_intent: Headline '94.2% agreement' shrinks to a side label 'routing statistic'; new lead '5.8% of items required human adjudication'.

show.event: routing statistic, not a quality metric

beats.role_note: Funnel with an arithmetic check '8,053 + 108 = 8,161'; chips: Wikipedia dump date · GO API date · model versions · temperatures; '25 hours'.
beats.narration_text: I also traced the pipeline as a funnel with arithmetic checks at every step, like 8,053 plus 108 equals 8,161, and added what anyone needs to reproduce it: dump and API dates, model versions and temperature settings. That was 25 hours.
beats.visual_intent: Funnel with an arithmetic check '8,053 + 108 = 8,161'; chips: Wikipedia dump date · GO API date · model versions · temperatures; '25 hours'.

show.event: dump date · API date · model versions · temperatures

beats.narration_text: My professor also flagged an ethics gap I hadn't seen: do students know these definitions are AI-generated? That paragraph is in now. CRITIQ helped me make the fixes; it didn't find them.
